questions.q: What is a protocol, such as HTTP?
questions.explain: HTTP is a set of rules for the text a client and a server send each other over a connection. Under the neat req object there is only that text.
options: An agreement about who says what, and in which format
A program that must be installed on every server
A kind of encryption for web traffic
The name of the cable between two computers

questions.q: In which order do the parts of an HTTP request arrive?
questions.explain: First POST /tasks?done=false HTTP/1.1, then one name: value header per line, then an empty line meaning "headers finished", then the body.
options: Request line, headers, an empty line, then the body
Headers, body, then the request line
Body, an empty line, then the headers
Request line, body, then the headers

questions.q: What are the three pieces of the request line POST /tasks?done=false HTTP/1.1?
questions.explain: The request line says what to do (POST), to what (/tasks?done=false) and which version of the rules is used (HTTP/1.1). The host goes in the host header.
options: The method, the path with its query string, and the HTTP version
The host, the port and the body
The method, the host name and the status code
The path, the content type and the body length

questions.q: How does HTTP end each line of the request line and the headers?
questions.explain: Every line ends with \r\n, and an empty line (\r\n on its own) ends the headers. The lesson prints them as text so you can see them.
options: With two characters: carriage return and line feed, \r\n
With a single \n, like a Linux text file
With a semicolon
It does not use lines; everything is JSON

questions.q: This splits a raw request the way the rules describe. What does it print?
questions.explain: The empty line (\r\n\r\n) separates the head from the body. The first line of the head is the request line; the other three are headers. The body is the 20 bytes of JSON that Content-Length promised.
options:
POST /tasks?done=false HTTP/1.1
3 20

POST /tasks HTTP/1.1
3 20

POST /tasks?done=false HTTP/1.1
4 20

POST /tasks?done=false HTTP/1.1
3 0

questions.q: A raw connection asks a node:http server for /tasks. What does this print?
questions.explain: The status line is version, code and reason phrase. The body has 16 characters but 17 bytes, because é takes two bytes in UTF-8, and Content-Length counts bytes.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: è, û and é each take two bytes in UTF-8, so 12 characters are 15 bytes. Content-Length must be the byte count, which Buffer.byteLength gives you.

questions.q: A server sets Content-Length to body.length for a body that contains é. What is wrong?
questions.explain: With a length that is too small, the client stops reading early and the body is cut. Use Buffer.byteLength(body), or leave the header out and let Node send the body in chunks.
options: body.length counts characters, but Content-Length must count bytes, so the number is too small
Nothing: characters and bytes are always the same
Content-Length must count lines, not characters
The header must be written in lower case

questions.q: In the output of curl -v, what do lines starting with > and < show?
questions.explain: Lines with * are curl's notes, > lines go out, < lines come back. That makes curl -v the first tool to reach for when an API surprises you.
options: > is the request curl sent; < is the response it got
> is the response; < is the request
> are errors; < are warnings
Both show curl's own notes about the connection

questions.q: What does Connection: keep-alive mean in a response?
questions.explain: Opening a connection takes time. Keep-alive reuses it, which is faster. Node adds this header by itself.
options: The connection stays open for the next request instead of being rebuilt each time
The server will restart if it crashes
The client must send a request every 5 seconds
The response is cached for later

questions.explain: Header names are not case sensitive, and Headers.get ignores case. But req.headers in node:http is a plain object with lower-case keys, so reading it with capitals gives undefined. Always read lower case.

questions.q: Which Content-Type does a classic HTML form send by default?
questions.explain: A media type names the body's format: application/json for JSON, text/html for a page, text/plain for plain text, and application/x-www-form-urlencoded for a classic form.
options: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
application/json
text/html
text/plain

"application/json" true
"application/json" true
"text/plain" false
"" false

questions.q: A client sends Content-Type: text/plain to an endpoint that only accepts JSON. Which status fits?
questions.explain: 415 means "I do not accept this format". 400 is for a body in the right format that the server cannot use, such as broken JSON or a missing title.
options: 415 Unsupported Media Type
400 Bad Request
404 Not Found
500 Internal Server Error

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: {title: 'Buy milk'} is valid JavaScript but not JSON, which needs double quotes around names and strings, so JSON.parse throws a SyntaxError. {"title": 42} parses, but a title must be text.
options:
201 title check
400 SyntaxError
400 title check

201 title check
201 title check
400 title check

201 title check
400 SyntaxError
201 title check

201 title check
400 TypeError
400 title check

questions.q: This is the lesson's JSON-body server, called four times. What does it print?
questions.explain: The charset parameter is fine, because only the part before ; is compared. null is valid JSON but has no title, and body?.title copes with it: 400. text/html is refused with 415. A title of only spaces is empty after trimming: 400.

questions.q: The lesson's JSON server reads the whole body with for await. What does a real server add?
questions.explain: A body is outside input. Count the bytes as they arrive and stop with 413 once the limit is passed.
options: A limit on how many bytes it reads, so nobody can send a gigabyte of "JSON"
A second JSON.parse, to be sure
A check that the body is shorter than the URL
Nothing: for await stops at 1 MB by itself

questions.q: HTTP does not remember anything between two requests. How does "you are still logged in" work?
questions.explain: A cookie is a small piece of text the browser remembers for the server. Set-Cookie sets it; the browser returns it in the Cookie header.
options: The server sets a cookie, and the browser sends it back on every later request
The server remembers the client's IP address forever
The connection stays open for as long as you are logged in
The browser sends the password with every request

questions.q: What does the HttpOnly cookie attribute protect against?
questions.explain: HttpOnly hides the cookie from document.cookie. Sending only over HTTPS is Secure; blocking most cross-site requests is SameSite.
options: JavaScript on the page cannot read the cookie, so an injected script cannot steal the session
The cookie cannot be sent over plain HTTP
Other websites cannot send the cookie with their requests
The cookie cannot be changed by the server

questions.q: What does the Secure cookie attribute do?
questions.explain: Secure is about the connection, not the value: over HTTPS, the whole request is encrypted. It does not hide the value from the user, who can still see and edit it.
options: The browser sends the cookie only over HTTPS, never over plain HTTP where others on the network could read it
It encrypts the cookie's value
It stops JavaScript from reading the cookie
It makes the cookie last forever

questions.q: Which cookie attribute blocks many cross-site request forgery (CSRF) attacks?
questions.explain: With SameSite=Lax, the browser does not send the cookie with most requests started by other sites. None turns that protection off (and needs Secure).
options: SameSite=Lax
Path=/
Max-Age=3600
SameSite=None

questions.q: A cookie is set without Max-Age and without Expires. When does it disappear?
questions.explain: Without Max-Age, it is a session cookie that lasts until the browser closes. Max-Age=3600 keeps it for 3600 seconds, and Max-Age=0 deletes it at once.
options: When the browser closes
After exactly one hour
Never
After the next request

questions.q: After login, what should the server put in the cookie?
questions.explain: The user can edit their own cookies, so a role or id in a cookie can be changed to anyone else's. A random id that only means something in the server's session store gives nothing away and cannot be guessed.
options: A long random session id, and keep the user's data on the server
user=ada; role=admin, so the server does not need to look anything up
The user's id number, such as uid=42
The user's password, so the next login is automatic

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: encodeURIComponent turns ;, the space and = into %3B, %20 and %3D. Without it, the value would sneak in an extra admin=1 part. Seven days is 604,800 seconds.
options: lang=en%3B%20admin%3D1; Path=/; Max-Age=604800; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax
lang=en; admin=1; Path=/; Max-Age=604800; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax
lang=en%3B%20admin%3D1; Path=/; Max-Age=7; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax
lang=en%3B admin%3D1; Path=/; Max-Age=604800; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The parser splits on the first = only, because a value (like base64) may contain more. A part with no = is skipped, and a missing header gives an empty object.
options:
{"token":"a=b==","theme":"dark mode"}
{}

{"token":"a","theme":"dark mode"}
{}

{"token":"a=b==","theme":"dark%20mode","broken":""}
{}

{"token":"a=b==","theme":"dark mode"}
undefined

questions.q: The session server finds the sid cookie with a regular expression. What does this print?
questions.explain: (?:^|;\s*) makes sid start a cookie, so xsid does not count. [^;]+ stops at the next ;. When nothing matches, ?.[1] gives undefined.
options:
abc123
undefined
undefined

abc123
evil
undefined

abc123; lang=en
undefined
undefined

abc123

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Login answers 204 with a cookie holding a random id. Sending that cookie back finds the session. A guessed id such as sid=1 is not in the store, and no cookie at all is not either: both get 401.

questions.q: GET /me/orders returns the logged-in customer's orders. Which Cache-Control header fits?
questions.explain: Personal data must not be kept by shared caches such as a CDN, which could hand one customer's orders to the next person who asks for the same URL. no-store tells every cache to keep no copy. public, max-age=86400 is for things that are the same for everyone, such as a logo.
options: Cache-Control: no-store
Cache-Control: public, max-age=86400
Cache-Control: max-age=3600, because orders rarely change
None: browsers never cache API responses

questions.q: Which HTTP methods are safe (they only read)?
questions.explain: Safe methods never change anything on the server, so browsers, caches and search engines may call them freely.
options: GET, HEAD and OPTIONS
GET, PUT and DELETE
POST and PATCH
Every method is safe over HTTPS

questions.q: A developer adds GET /tasks/7/delete to delete a task from a link. Why is that a bad idea?
questions.explain: Tools follow GET links on their own because GET is supposed to only read. Changes belong in POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE.
options: GET must be safe: a link preview, a prefetch or a search engine could follow the link and delete the task
A GET URL cannot contain a number
GET requests cannot be answered with 204
It is fine, as long as the link is hidden

questions.q: A mobile app sends PUT /tasks/1 and the network drops before the answer arrives. Why is it safe to send it again?
questions.explain: PUT replaces the task with the same data each time. Retrying a POST is different: it could create a second task.
options: PUT is idempotent: sending it twice has the same effect as sending it once
PUT is safe: it never changes anything
The server ignores the second request automatically
It is not safe; PUT must never be retried

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Two POSTs made two tasks; two PUTs left one task in the same state. DELETE is idempotent too: the second call answers 404, but the state is the same, one task left.
options:
2 Call Ada
204 404 1

1 Call Ada
204 404 0

2 Call Ada
204 204 0

4 Call Ada
204 404 3

questions.q: Why does a browser warn you before it resends a form, but reloads a normal page without asking?
questions.explain: Resending a POST could buy something twice or create a duplicate. Repeating a GET only reads again.
options: A form is usually a POST, which is not idempotent; a page is a GET, which is safe
Forms are larger than pages
Pages are cached, forms are not
Forms use HTTPS and pages do not

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The first digit gives the class, so a client knows roughly what happened even for a code it has never seen. 429 (too many requests) is the client's side: it must slow down.
options: success, redirection, client error, client error, server error
success, success, client error, server error, server error
success, redirection, server error, client error, server error
informational, redirection, client error, client error, server error

questions.q: A client gets an error and wonders whether to try again unchanged. Which is right?
questions.explain: A 4xx means the request itself was wrong: fix it first. A 5xx means the server failed, which may be temporary, such as a database that is restarting.
options: After a 5xx, trying again later can work; after a 4xx, the same request will fail again
After a 4xx, trying again later can work; after a 5xx, it never will
Both should be retried at once, many times
Neither should ever be retried

questions.q: A response has status 301 Moved Permanently. Where should the client look?
questions.explain: 3xx codes mean "it is somewhere else", and Location gives the address. A deleted resource is 404 (or 410).
options: In the Location header, which says where the thing is now
In the body, which contains the new page
In the Content-Type header
Nowhere: 301 means the resource was deleted

questions.q: A client tries to create a task with a title that must be unique and is already used. Which status fits best?
questions.explain: 409 means the request clashes with the current state. 429 is what a rate limiter sends when a client sends too many requests.
options: 409 Conflict
429 Too Many Requests
415 Unsupported Media Type
503 Service Unavailable

questions.q: Your code throws an unexpected error while handling a request. What should the client receive?
questions.explain: A 500 is your bug, not the client's. Stack traces can reveal file paths and internals, so log them on the server and never send them.
options: 500 with a short generic message; the stack trace goes to the server log only
500 with the stack trace, so the client can report the bug
400, because the request caused the error
200 with an empty body, so nothing looks broken

questions.q: Finish parseRequest(raw). Split the head from the body at the empty line (\r\n\r\n). The first head line is METHOD TARGET VERSION. Each other head line is Name: value; store it with the name in lower case and the value trimmed. Return { method, target, headers, body }.
questions.explain: Find the empty line first. Split the head on \r\n; the first line is the request line. For headers, split on the first : only (a value such as localhost:3000 contains another), and lower-case the name, like node:http does.

questions.q: Finish isJson(contentType). Return true when the media type, the part before any ;, trimmed and in lower case, is exactly application/json. A missing header gives false.
questions.explain: Use ?? "" for a missing header, cut off the parameters at ;, then compare exactly. startsWith("application/json") would wrongly accept application/jsonp.

questions.q: Finish createStatus(contentType, text) like the lesson's server. Return 415 when the media type is not application/json, 400 when JSON.parse fails, 400 when title is not a string that is non-empty after trimming, and 201 otherwise.
questions.explain: Check the format first, then parse inside try/catch, then validate the field. body?.title handles a body of null.

questions.q: Finish sessionCookie(id, days) and clearSessionCookie(). The first returns a Set-Cookie value for sid (encoded with encodeURIComponent) with Path=/, Max-Age in seconds, HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite=Lax, in that order and joined with "; ". The second deletes it: an empty value and Max-Age=0, with the same other attributes.
questions.explain: Max-Age is in seconds: 7 × 24 × 60 × 60 = 604,800. The clearing cookie must have the same name and Path, or the browser treats it as a different cookie.
questions.expected:
sid=3f9c%202a; Path=/; Max-Age=604800; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax
sid=; Path=/; Max-Age=0; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax

questions.q: Finish parseCookies(header). Split the header on ;. For each part, split on the first = only, trim the name and value, and decode the value with decodeURIComponent. Skip parts without =. A missing header gives {}.
questions.explain: indexOf("=") finds the first =; slice before and after it keeps any further = in the value. header ?? "" handles a request with no cookies.

questions.q: Finish describe(method). Return "safe" for GET, HEAD and OPTIONS; "idempotent" for PUT and DELETE; and "neither" for anything else, such as POST and PATCH.
questions.explain: Safe methods only read (and are idempotent too). PUT and DELETE change data but can be repeated with the same effect. POST is neither, and PATCH is not guaranteed to be idempotent.
questions.expected:
GET safe
POST neither
PUT idempotent
PATCH neither
DELETE idempotent
HEAD safe

questions.q: Finish answer(method) for /tasks, which supports GET and POST. Return { status: 200 } for GET, { status: 201 } for POST, and for any other method { status: 405, allow: "GET, POST" }.
questions.explain: A known path with an unsupported method gets 405, and the Allow header tells the client which methods would work.
